keys.statement: Design from the reactor outwards: choose reactor and catalyst first, then add separations and recycles, because the reaction step sets the purity reached and how hard the purification will be.

plain.title: Design from the reactor outwards
plain.do: Choose the reactor and catalyst first, then add the separations and recycles.
plain.why: The reactor effluent defines the separation problem: the reaction step sets the purity reached and how hard purification will be.
plain.check: Fix the reactor outlet composition before designing the separation train.

decisions.mechanism: The reactor effluent defines the separation problem.
decisions.operation: Fix reactor and catalyst before the separation train.
decisions.expected_change: A separation train matched to the effluent.

keys.statement: Large plants run continuously; a single stirred tank does not reach batch productivity, but stirred tanks in series do.

plain.title: Large continuous plant: stirred tanks in series, not one tank
plain.when: A continuous reactor gives lower conversion than the batch process.
plain.why: One tank is fully back-mixed; tanks in series approach plug flow and batch-like conversion.
plain.check: In CHEPTA, compare the conversion of one, two and three stirred tanks of the same total volume.

decisions.obstacle: Continuous reactor with lower conversion than batch.
decisions.mechanism: Back-mixing in one tank; series tanks approach plug flow.

keys.statement: For mixtures with polar components such as glycerol, methanol and water, use NRTL or UNIQUAC, filling missing binary pairs with UNIFAC estimates.

plain.title: Polar mixtures such as glycerol, methanol and water: NRTL or UNIQUAC, with UNIFAC for missing pairs
plain.when: A mixture contains polar components and some binary parameters are missing.
plain.do: Use an activity-coefficient model, NRTL or UNIQUAC, and fill the missing binary pairs with UNIFAC (group-contribution) estimates, as Pasha et al. 2021 describe.
plain.why: Activity models describe non-ideal liquids; UNIFAC fills the gaps.
plain.check: Estimated pairs are guesses until checked against data: find out which pairs CHEPTA has from data and which are predicted.

decisions.obstacle: Polar, non-ideal mixtures and missing parameters.
decisions.mechanism: Activity models describe non-ideal liquids; UNIFAC fills gaps.
decisions.operation: Activity-coefficient model with estimated missing pairs.
limits: Estimated pairs are guesses until checked against data (see the Palomar and Li 2017 rows).

keys.statement: Reactors in series with decanters between them remove a heavy liquid product (glycerol) as it forms and allow a reactant to be added in stages.

plain.title: Heavy liquid product limits conversion: reactors in series with decanters between them
plain.when: A heavy product phase (glycerol in biodiesel) limits conversion, and a reactant harms the catalyst at high concentration.
plain.do: Put decanters between reactors in series to remove the product phase as it forms, and add the reactant in stages.
plain.why: Removing the product phase and dosing the reactant keep conditions favourable for conversion and catalyst life.
plain.check: In CHEPTA, set phases: "VLL" on the decanters and check that the glycerol phase separates.

keys.statement: Pinch-based heat integration of biodiesel plants cut heating and cooling utilities by roughly 11 to 16% in the cited studies.

plain.title: Biodiesel plants: pinch analysis cut utilities by about 11-16%
plain.when: A biodiesel plant with several distillation steps uses much heating and cooling.
plain.do: Apply pinch analysis (heat-recovery targeting) to match hot and cold streams.
plain.why: Matching hot and cold streams recovers heat.
plain.check: Compare your utility use with the pinch targets.
plain.result: Heating and cooling utilities fell by roughly 11 to 16% in studies cited by Pasha et al. 2021, not read by Lab.

decisions.obstacle: Utility use of several distillation steps.
decisions.mechanism: Matching hot and cold streams recovers heat.
